beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Aravind Ravi, and this pitch is read by a synthetic voice. When you own an AI feature, a judge model scores it against your rubric. So the question isn't only whether my feature passes. It's whether the judge reads my rubric the way I meant it.

beats.narration_text: It's called Readback. It will show a product manager which clause of their eval rubric an AI judge reads differently than they meant. When it's done, it will be a Python repository with a command-line tool, a case study on public meeting data, and a log of judge agreement before and after a revision.

shot.visual_intent: A rubric page with five clause lines stands on the stage; a judge figure reads it; one clause line lifts out and gets a terracotta tape marker; a small repository box with a terminal prompt drops in beside it.
shot.motion_claim: A rubric page with five clause lines stands on the stage; a judge figure reads it; one clause line lifts out and gets a terracotta tape marker; a small repository box with a terminal prompt drops in beside it.

qc.sparse_reason: show-tell style: one drawn scene on a cream stage per beat, minimal labels, the voice carries the explanation; only underfill and clustered are waived.

beats.narration_text: Why care? If the judge misreads a clause, the scores look fine and the ship decision is wrong. I looked at two tools. Maxim AI measures how well several judges agree with humans. Ork dot AI compares an evaluator with human labels, then rewrites its prompt. As far as I could find in their docs on October fourteenth, neither says which clause caused the disagreement. Readback will, and it will ask the P M about that clause instead of rewriting it.

beats.narration_text: The reader is a hiring manager for AI product roles. In the first minute, they'll open the README and see one table: per-clause agreement with my labels, the clause that disagreed most, the question Readback will ask, my revision, and held-out agreement before and after. The end user is a P M with their own rubric.

beats.narration_text: What does it prove? That I treat a rubric as a prompt contract, and verify instead of trust: my labels will be committed before any judge runs, so the git history proves the order. That I'll evaluate per clause on held-out data, and ground claims in transcript lines. A reviewer could conclude I understand why judges need a human anchor. Not that it works for every feature. I'll test one.

beats.narration_text: In: the rubric module, and a case study on ten public AMI meetings, where teams role-play product design. Out: Readback will never rewrite a rubric itself. It asks, and the P M decides. First: one rubric, three judges, and my labels, producing an agreement table. You'll know it ran because its commit comes after my labels' commit.

beats.narration_text: What could sink it? Overfitting: revising the rubric until the judges agree on the examples I tuned it on. So I'll freeze a held-out set first, and report only held-out numbers. And because judges can share blind spots, I'll compare same-model and cross-model judges, and report it either way.

beats.narration_text: Why this project? It's a mix. New to me: eval design, judge and human agreement, and multi-model judging. Already mine: writing product requirements, as a P M at L G Energy Solution Vertech, Tech for Dev and Koine Arth, though those documents are internal. From this course: my week one film verified every on-screen number, and I held my week two recipe at draft while to-do items were open. I think e-vals are becoming core to AI PM work, and I don't have an eval project yet.
